_comment: A fictional cover letter in the owner's rubric shape (WP12 round 6): greeting, hook whose first sentence carries a digit, a one-campaign proof with its constraint and tradeoff, a paragraph on the employer with a first step, and a two-sentence close with the profile link. $FACT, $JOB, $CONTACT and $STORY are replaced by the test's ids; an absent id is dropped.

sentences.text: In 2024 I grew online orders by 35% for a regional bakery chain after rebuilding how its paid search conversions were counted.
Your paid search program ties spend decisions to reported results, and that rebuild at the bakery chain is the work I would bring to it first.
When I took over the bakery chain's account, its dashboard counted every phone call as an order, so the budget kept flowing to searches that never produced a sale.
I rebuilt the tracking so that only paid orders counted, which halved the reported conversions for two months and made the owner nervous about the spend for most of that spring.
I held the budget flat through that dip and moved money toward the searches that still produced paid orders.
By the end of 2024 online orders were up 35%, and the owner had stopped reading the dashboard in favour of my weekly report.
Your posting asks for someone who owns paid search strategy and reports results to the sales team, which is the weekly rhythm I kept for the bakery chain's store managers.
Those managers used my report to decide which of their locations received more budget the following week, and two of them started asking for it before Monday.
A sales team reads the same numbers with a different question, so I would keep the report short and tie every line to a closed sale.
First I would audit which of your paid search conversions reach the sales team's records, the step that paid off at the bakery chain.
My work and references are on my profile at https://www.linkedin.example/in/avery-example.
I can walk you through the bakery chain's order data on a call this week.
